narrative_story:
# The Last Watch of the *Mara Celeste*

---

People always ask the wrong question. They ask, *Were you afraid?*

No one ever asks what I made for dinner that last night, or whether the captain took milk in her tea toward the end when the powdered stuff was all we had left, or what card she was holding when the portside pump seized and the engine room went quiet in a way that engine rooms should never go quiet. No one asks the right questions because no one wants the true answers, which are: canned tomato soup with saltines, no she drank it black, and the seven of diamonds, which she laid down on the galley table with a hand that did not shake, and said, *Gin*, and I said, *That's forty-three games to you and eleven to me, and you are a relentless cheat, Captain*, and the black water outside rose another six inches up the glass.

That is how a ship dies. Not all at once. In inches.

---

My name is Dolores Yuen. Ship's cook, *Mara Celeste*, registration Port of Manila, though she hadn't been home in nine years and neither had I. I have been cook on five vessels and I have outlived one of them, which is the one I am telling you about now, here in this room that smells of antiseptic and floor wax, while the man from the maritime commission clicks his pen and waits for me to say something useful.

I will try.

But you have to understand that nothing about the end of the *Mara Celeste* was useful. Nothing was efficient or heroic or cautionary. It was just a woman who loved a boat more than the boat loved her, and the sea that took them both, and me in the galley boiling water because I did not know what else to do with my hands.

---

The typhoon had a name. They always do. Typhoon Lannie, which sounds like a girl I went to school with in Cebu City who stole my lunch money and broke the clasp on my St. Christopher medal. The meteorological service in Guam posted the warning seventy-two hours before it arrived, and we heard it, we all heard it—Chief Engineer Salcedo and First Mate Bautista and the two deckhands, Reyes and Little Reyes, who were not related but whom we called Big and Little because one was six foot three and the other was five foot nothing and this was a ship of unimaginative people.

Bautista spread the weather charts on the bridge table and traced the projected path with his finger and said, *Captain, if we divert southeast we can make Bermuda by Thursday.*

And Captain Wen looked at those charts the way a woman looks at a letter she has already read too many times, and she said, *No.*

And Bautista said, *Captain.*

And she said, *I know who is in Bermuda, Dante. I know exactly who is in Bermuda.*

She did not look at him when she said it. She was looking out through the bridge windows at a sea that was still deceptively calm, that pale green glass you get in the Sargasso when the weed thins out and the depth below is so enormous it turns the water the color of jade. She was gripping the wheel housing with both hands. Not steering. Just holding.

Bautista looked at me. I don't know why people looked at me in those moments. I was the cook. I made rice and I made coffee and I made sure the dry stores were rotated properly and I played cards with the captain because nobody else would. I had no authority. I had a galley and a temper and a collection of recipes clipped from women's magazines that I kept in a binder with a cracked spine, and none of these things were useful in a crisis of navigation.

But he looked at me, and I looked at her, and she looked at the sea, and that was the chain of looking that held the *Mara Celeste* together in those final days. Everyone looking at the next person, hoping someone would say the thing that needed saying.

No one did.

---

I should tell you about the boat.

The *Mara Celeste* was a sixty-eight-foot cargo vessel, steel-hulled, built in 1971 at a yard in Kaohsiung that no longer exists. She had been a fishing trawler, then a coastal freighter, then a supply runner for the offshore rigs, then a cargo hauler for whoever would hire her. She was old. Her keel was sound but her plating was tired. There were places in the lower hold where you could press your thumb against the steel and feel it give, just slightly, like the skin of a fruit going soft.

Captain Wen's grandfather had bought her in 1985 with money he'd saved working the tuna fleet out of General Santos. He named her after his wife, who had been dead eleven years and whose name was not actually Celeste but something else, something in Hokkien that I never learned, but he liked the way *Celeste* looked painted on the transom in white letters. He said it looked like a word that belonged on the sea.

The boat passed to Wen's mother, who did not want it, and then to Wen, who wanted nothing else.

I learned this in pieces, over months, over games of gin rummy played on a table that was bolted to the galley floor. Captain Wen did not tell stories. She released facts, one at a time, the way a doctor releases bad news: carefully, watching your face to see how much you could take.

*My grandfather could navigate by stars alone.*

*My mother sold the house to keep the registration current.*

*The bank says the vessel is worth more as scrap.*

She said these things between hands of cards, between sips of tea, between radio checks and course corrections and all the other small machinery of a life lived at sea. She said them without emphasis. She said them the way you state the weather. *Clear skies. Twelve-knot wind from the east. The bank wants to sell my grandfather's boat for scrap.*

---

The letters had started eight months before.

I know because I was the one who collected the mail when we docked. I was the one who carried the bundle to her cabin and set it on her desk beside the sextant that had belonged to her grandfather, the one she never used for navigation but kept polished to a mirror shine, its brass bright as a small sun.

The first letter was from a maritime lending company in Singapore. The second was from a law firm in Hong Kong. The third, fourth, fifth—these accumulated in a stack she kept beneath a glass paperweight shaped like a turtle, and I watched that stack grow the way you watch a waterline rise.

She stopped smiling after the third letter. I noted this because I noted everything about Captain Wen, not out of devotion, though there was devotion, but out of the particular attention that a cook pays to the people she feeds. You learn to read appetite. You learn to read the difference between a person who is not hungry and a person who has forgotten that hunger exists. Captain Wen stopped being hungry around the time the letters started and never started again, and I began making smaller portions so she would not notice how little she was eating, and she did not notice, and this was its own kind of grief.

She was forty-one. She had been at sea since she was seventeen. She had a scar on her left forearm from a mooring line that snapped in Davao and a tattoo on her right shoulder of a compass rose that pointed, she said, to nowhere in particular. She wore her hair short and her shirts buttoned to the collar and she played gin rummy with a ruthlessness that bordered on the spiritual.

She was the best captain I ever served, and I say this knowing full well she killed the *Mara Celeste* and damn near killed us all, and I say it anyway.

---

The first day of Lannie was a lesson in physics.

The sea does not simply rise. It reorganizes. The swells come first, long and muscular, rolling under the hull like the breathing of something alive. Then the wind finds its voice—not all at once but in octaves, building from a moan to a howl to a sound that has no name, a sound that presses against your eardrums until you feel it in your teeth.

I secured the galley at 0600. Lashed the pots, locked the stove gimbals, stowed everything breakable and strapped down everything heavy. I had been through storms before. I knew the choreography. What I did not know was how it felt to go through a storm on a ship whose captain had chosen not to run.

Bautista tried again that morning. I heard them on the bridge, their voices rising and falling beneath the wind. Bautista was a good man. He was from Iloilo and he had three daughters whose photographs were taped above his bunk and he believed in procedure the way religious people believe in God—absolutely, without evidence that it would save him.

*We can still make Bermuda,* he said. *Sixteen hours at full steam.*

*And who is waiting at the dock in Bermuda, Dante?*

*That is not the relevant question, Captain.*

*It is the only question.*

I heard something break. A coffee mug, maybe, or the barometer glass. Then silence, then Bautista's footsteps descending the bridge ladder, and he passed the galley without looking in and I pretended to be counting cans of beans because we were both pretending, all of us were pretending, and the pretending was load-bearing.

---

I should tell you about the repo men because the repo men are the point, or near enough.

Two weeks before, we had docked in Nassau to offload a cargo of machine parts bound for a desalination plant. While we were tied up, a man in a white linen suit came aboard without asking and handed Captain Wen an envelope and said, *You have thirty days to surrender the vessel or we will impound her in the next port of registry.*

He said it standing on her deck. On her grandfather's deck. He had leather shoes that were wrong for a ship and a clipboard and the particular smile of a person who represents an institution and has confused the institution's power with his own.

Wen read the document. She folded it. She put it in her shirt pocket.

*Bermuda,* she said. *You want me to bring her to Bermuda.*

*It would be simplest,* the man said.

*Simplest,* she repeated, tasting the word like something gone off.

*The company has contracted a salvage assessor. He'll meet you at the Royal Naval Dockyard. It's quite painless, I'm told.*

Painless. He said *painless* about taking a woman's grandfather's boat and selling it for scrap to cover a debt that existed because fuel costs had tripled and cargo rates had halved and the maritime lending company in Singapore charged interest the way a fire charges a forest—consuming everything and calling it natural.

Wen said nothing. She walked the man to the gangway and watched him step onto the dock and she stood there for a long time after he was gone, and I brought her tea, and she drank it, and neither of us said a word about the man in the white suit, and the *Mara Celeste* departed Nassau three hours later on a heading that was not Bermuda.

It was never going to be Bermuda.

---

The second day of Lannie was when the ship began to speak.

I do not mean this metaphorically. Steel under stress makes sounds that have no analogue on land. The hull groaned. The frames shrieked. The rivets along the waterline—original 1971 rivets, because who had money for re-riveting—made a percussive ticking that sounded like a counting-down, though of what, to what, I tried not to consider.

The waves were thirty feet by noon. Forty by evening. The *Mara Celeste* climbed each one with a shudder and fell into each trough with a concussion that rattled my teeth and sent the canned goods jumping on their shelves despite the restraints.

I made tea at 1400 and brought it to the bridge. Wen was at the wheel, which was manual now—the autopilot had failed at dawn, a fuse blown by a power surge, and she was steering by hand, by feel, reading the water through the soles of her boots the way her grandfather had taught her, or so I imagined, because she never said this directly, she only said once, *He could feel a current change through the deck plates*, and I understood this to mean she could too.

I set the tea on the console. It slid. I caught it. Set it again in the cup holder that Reyes had welded from a tin can.

*You should eat,* I said.

*I ate.*

*You did not eat. I know what you ate because I am the one who makes what you eat and you did not eat because I did not make anything because the stove is bucking like a horse and I cannot keep a pot level. But I can make sandwiches. I can make sandwiches in the apocalypse, Captain, this is my skill, and I am asking you to let me use it.*

She looked at me. The navigation lights were out and the bridge was lit only by the emergency strips, that pale green chemical glow that makes everyone look drowned. In that light her face was all planes and shadows, her jaw set, her eyes the color of nothing.

*Peanut butter,* she said.

*Peanut butter,* I confirmed.

I went below and made peanut butter sandwiches in a galley that was trying to kill me, bracing myself between the counter and the bulkhead while the ship rolled thirty degrees to port and thirty degrees to starboard in a rhythm that was almost, almost, almost predictable, and then was not, and I bit my tongue and tasted blood and thought: *This is how Dolores Yuen dies, making a sandwich.*

I did not die. I brought the sandwiches. She ate one. The tea went cold.

That was when I started counting the teas. The cold teas. The ones I brought that she did not drink because she could not take her hands off the wheel, or would not, and they sat on the console growing cold while the storm screamed and the *Mara Celeste* fought and I stood in the bridge doorway holding a dish towel because I had nothing else to hold.

Four teas went cold that day. I poured each one out in the galley sink and made a new one and brought it up and it went cold too, and this was the rhythm of the second day: tea, storm, tea, storm, the hull crying, the wind crying, Captain Wen not crying, and me in between, carrying mugs.

---

At 2200 on the second night, Bautista came to the galley.

He sat at the bolted table and put his head in his hands and said, *The bilge pumps are running at capacity.*

I set a mug in front of him. Coffee, not tea. Tea was for the captain. This was a distinction I maintained without deciding to.

*How long?* I asked.

*At this rate? Twelve hours before the water reaches the engine mounts. Maybe less. Salcedo thinks less.*

*And the auxiliary pumps?*

*One is working. One is not. Salcedo is trying.*

He lifted his head. He looked at me with the eyes of a man who had three daughters and a wife in Iloilo and a future that was becoming past tense while he sat in a galley drinking coffee he did not want.

*She will not turn for Bermuda,* he said.

*No.*

*She will not signal for rescue.*

*I don't know.*

*Dolores.* He
